facts.statement: Gracilisuchus is an extinct genus of tiny pseudosuchians from the Late Triassic of Argentina.
facts.quote: Gracilisuchus (meaning "slender crocodile") is an extinct genus of tiny pseudosuchian (a group which includes the ancestors of crocodilians) from the Late Triassic of Argentina.

facts.statement: The only species, G. stipanicicorum, belongs to the clade Suchia, which is close to the ancestry of crocodylomorphs.
facts.quote: It contains a single species, G. stipanicicorum, which is placed in the clade Suchia, close to the ancestry of crocodylomorphs.

facts.statement: Alfred Romer first described both the genus and the species in 1972.
facts.quote: Both the genus and the species were first described by Alfred Romer in 1972.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen is now housed at the Museum of Paleontology at the National University of La Rioja with the number PULR 08.
facts.quote: The specimen has since been transferred to the Museum of Paleontology at the National University of La Rioja (PULR), where it bears the specimen number PULR 08.

facts.statement: Romer described the specimens in the journal Breviora in 1972.
facts.quote: In 1972, Romer described the specimens his team had discovered in the journal Breviora.

facts.statement: The species name G. stipanicicorum honors the work of Pedro and Maria Stipanicic in the stratigraphy and paleobotany of the Triassic period.
facts.quote: Furthermore, he placed them in the type and only species G. stipanicicorum, which honors the work of Pedro and Maria Stipanicic in the stratigraphy and paleobotany of the Triassic period.

facts.statement: Gracilisuchus was a small member of the Pseudosuchia.
facts.quote: Gracilisuchus was a small member of the Pseudosuchia.

facts.statement: The largest skull measures slightly over 9 cm in length, and the largest femur is roughly 8 cm long.
facts.quote: The largest skull has a length of slightly over 9 cm, and the largest femur has a length of roughly 8 cm.

facts.statement: The estimated weight of Gracilisuchus is 1.31 kg.
facts.quote: The weight of Gracilisuchus has been estimated at 1.31 kg.

facts.statement: A scleral ring exists within the eye socket, where the ossicles contact but do not overlap each other.
facts.quote: Within the eye socket, there is a scleral ring, and the ossicles (bony segments) comprising the ring contact but do not overlap each other.

facts.statement: A small, triangular postparietal bone is present.
facts.quote: There is also a postparietal bone, which is small and triangular.

facts.statement: Gracilisuchus has four teeth in the premaxilla, unlike Turfanosuchus and Yonghesuchus which have five.
facts.quote: Also unlike Turfanosuchus and Yonghesuchus, Gracilisuchus has four teeth in the premaxilla instead of five, like Prestosuchus, Saurosuchus, Fasolasuchus, Batrachotomus, the Rauisuchidae, and the Crocodylomorpha.

facts.statement: The premaxillary teeth lack a cutting edge at the front and lack serrated denticles on either edge.
facts.quote: There is no cutting edge, or carina, at the front of the premaxillary teeth, and they lack serrated denticles on either the front or rear edges.

facts.statement: Gracilisuchus possessed eight vertebrae in its neck region.
facts.quote: There are eight cervical vertebrae.

facts.statement: The back of Gracilisuchus contained sixteen dorsal vertebrae.
facts.quote: There are sixteen dorsal vertebrae.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence confirms the presence of two sacral vertebrae in Gracilisuchus.
facts.quote: Two sacral vertebrae are known.

facts.statement: Gracilisuchus had at least sixteen vertebrae in its tail.
facts.quote: There were at least 16 caudal (tail) vertebrae.

facts.statement: The lower end of Gracilisuchus's upper arm bone was 2.5 times wider than its shaft.
facts.quote: The width of the bottom end of the humerus is 2.5 times that of the shaft

facts.statement: The two halves of Gracilisuchus's ischium were joined near the top, with the gap between them measuring only 22% of the bone's total length.
facts.quote: The articulation between the two halves of the ischium is characteristically close to the top of the bone, with the separated portion being only 22% the length of the bone

facts.statement: Approximately the bottom 55% of Gracilisuchus's thigh bone was curved into an S-shape.
facts.quote: Roughly the bottom 55% of the femur is bowed, resulting in a sigmoidal shape.

facts.statement: The shin bone of Gracilisuchus was 90% the length of its thigh bone.
facts.quote: The tibia is 90% of the femur's length

facts.statement: Gracilisuchus had five toes on its foot, with preserved bone counts of 2, 3, 2, 2, and 1 phalanges respectively.
facts.quote: There are five digits in the foot, with the number of phalanges being preserved on each digit being 2-3-2-2-1 from the first digit to the fifth

facts.statement: Gracilisuchus possessed a 'crocodile-normal' ankle joint where the astragalus and calcaneum bones were connected by a peg-and-socket mechanism.
facts.quote: Like Turfanosuchus and other members of the Crurotarsi, Gracilisuchus has a "crocodile-normal" ankle joint, with the astragalus and calcaneum being joined with a "peg-and-socket" joint.

facts.statement: Unlike some related species, the ankle bone of Gracilisuchus connected to the shin bone via a 'screw-joint' with slightly angled surfaces.
facts.quote: Unlike Turfanosuchus, Euparkeria, and Marasuchus, the astragalus has a "screw-joint" articulation with the tibia, with slightly divergent articulating surfaces.

facts.statement: Gracilisuchus had two rows of bony plates called osteoderms running from behind its skull over its neck and torso.
facts.quote: Gracilisuchus bore two rows of bony plates known as osteoderms above its neck and torso, with the first pair beginning immediately behind the skull.

facts.statement: The osteoderms of Gracilisuchus likely did not extend over the hips, possibly due to skeletal structure or preservation issues.
facts.quote: They do not appear to continue over the hip; this may be associated with the lack of "tables" in the neural spines of the rear vertebrae, or it may be an artifact of preservation.

facts.statement: Gracilisuchus osteoderms overlapped slightly and were arranged asymmetrically, with the left plate positioned slightly forward of the right.
facts.quote: Each osteoderm slightly overlaps the one immediately behind it, and the left osteoderm of each row is slightly further forward than the right, creating an asymmetrical appearance.

facts.statement: The front row of Gracilisuchus osteoderms was triangular, while those further back were leaf-shaped.
facts.quote: While osteoderms from the frontmost row are triangular, osteoderms further behind are leaf-shaped.

facts.statement: Each osteoderm of Gracilisuchus featured a longitudinal crest down the middle with a depression on either side.
facts.quote: The surface of each osteoderm bears a longitudinal midline crest, with a depression on either side.

facts.statement: Gracilisuchus osteoderms show variable surface textures, ranging from smooth to those with radial pits and grooves.
facts.quote: Different specimens of Gracilisuchus have different osteoderm surface textures; some are smooth like Turfanosuchus, while others bear radial pits and grooves like Erpetosuchus.

facts.statement: Romer classified Gracilisuchus as a clear relative of Ornithosuchus based on skull and skeletal similarities.
facts.quote: Romer considered Gracilisuchus to be, "quite clear[ly]", a relative of the Scottish Ornithosuchus, owing to similarities in skull structure and other skeletal features.

facts.statement: Romer debated the dinosaur classification of ornithosuchids, citing basal archosaur traits like the closed acetabulum and osteoderms in Gracilisuchus.
facts.quote: However, he had reservations regarding Walker's identification of ornithosuchids as dinosaurs, noting basal archosaur traits such as the closed acetabulum, osteoderms, and crocodile-normal ankle.

facts.statement: Arthur Cruickshank removed Gracilisuchus from Ornithosuchidae because it possessed a "crocodile-normal" ankle joint unlike other members of the family.
facts.quote: He observed that, while Gracilisuchus had a "crocodile-normal" joint, other ornithosuchids had a "crocodile-reversed" joint; he thus removed Gracilisuchus from the Ornithosuchidae.

facts.statement: Brinkman tentatively placed Gracilisuchus closer to crocodile-line archosaurs like Erythrosuchidae and Rauisuchidae rather than Ornithosuchids.
facts.quote: Thus, in a phylogenetic tree, Brinkman tentatively depicted Gracilisuchus as being closer to the "crocodile-line" Erythrosuchidae, the Rauisuchidae, and the Stagonolepididae (=Aetosauria) than the Ornithosuchidae and the Euparkeriidae.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis recovered Gracilisuchus as a member of Suchia, defined by a "crocodile-normal" ankle and other traits.
facts.quote: It was recovered as a member of the Suchia, a group defined by Bernard Krebs as being characterized by a "crocodile-normal" ankle, among other characteristics.

facts.statement: Paul Sereno removed Gracilisuchus from Ornithosuchids in 1991 and used it to define the contents of the group Suchia.
facts.quote: Sereno in 1991, when he removed Gracilisuchus from the ornithosuchids, and used it to define Suchia's contents.

facts.statement: Scientists have not reached a consensus on the evolutionary relationships between Gracilisuchus and other crurotarsans.
facts.quote: Subsequent analyses did not reach a consensus on the relationships between Gracilisuchus and other crurotarsans.

facts.statement: In 1994, Lars Juul placed Gracilisuchus inside Paracrocodylomorpha as the sister taxon of Postosuchus.
facts.quote: In a 1994 analysis, Lars Juul moved Gracilisuchus inside the Paracrocodylomorpha, placing it as the sister taxon of Postosuchus

facts.statement: A 2004 analysis by Benton found Gracilisuchus to be the sister taxon of the Phytosauria.
facts.quote: In an analysis for the 2004 second edition of The Dinosauria, Benton performed another phylogenetic analysis, finding Gracilisuchus to be the sister taxon of the Phytosauria

facts.statement: A 2014 analysis by Richard Butler named a group containing Gracilisuchus, Turfanosuchus, and Yonghesuchus as Gracilisuchidae.
facts.quote: In 2014, an analysis led by Richard Butler, modified from that of Nesbitt, suggested for the first time that Gracilisuchus formed a group with Turfanosuchus and Yonghesuchus, two basal suchians with similarly convoluted taxonomic histories. The group was named the Gracilisuchidae.

facts.statement: Gracilisuchus differed from other rauisuchians by lacking an ossification at the back of the top of the skull and a fenestra between the premaxilla and maxilla.
facts.quote: Parrish also noted that Gracilisuchus differed from other rauisuchians in the absence of an ossification at the back of the top of the skull, and the absence of a fenestra between the premaxilla and maxilla.

facts.statement: Analyses suggested that the squamosal flange of Gracilisuchus was homologous with that of Postosuchus and crocodylomorphs.
facts.quote: Both analyses suggested that the squamosal flange of Gracilisuchus was homologous with that of Postosuchus and crocodylomorphs.

facts.statement: Nesbitt noted that removing Turfanosuchus allied Gracilisuchus with ornithosuchids, based on traits like three premaxillary teeth and a pubis longer than the ischium.
facts.quote: He noted that the removal of Turfanosuchus allied Gracilisuchus with ornithosuchids in one possible tree, with this relationship being based upon unambiguous synapomorphies such as the presence of three premaxillary teeth; the length of the pubis being more than 70% that of the femur; the pubis being longer than the ischium; the presence of a midline gap at the bottom of the ischium; and the lack of a "hook" at the top end of the fifth metatarsal.

facts.statement: The relationship between Gracilisuchus and Yonghesuchus received poor support, partly due to incomplete material of Yonghesuchus.
facts.quote: However, poor support for this relationship was obtained, partially due to the incompleteness of material referred to Yonghesuchus.

facts.statement: Gracilisuchus is a genus of gracilisuchid archosauromorphs.
facts.quote: Gracilisuchus (lat. "cocodrilo grácil") es un género de arcosauromofos gracilisúquidos

facts.statement: The animal was small, measuring about 70 centimeters in length and 30 centimeters in height.
facts.quote: Animal de pequeñas dimensiones, media alrededor de 70 centímetros de largo por 30 de alto

facts.statement: Its skull was low and elongated, triangular in dorsal view with a very narrow anterior end and a wide base.
facts.quote: El cráneo es bajo y alargado, en vista dorsal es triangular, con el extremo anterior muy angosto y la base ancha

facts.statement: Its large eye orbits projected dorsally, suggesting lateral-dorsal and rostral eye placement.
facts.quote: Sus grandes órbitas oculares se proyectan hacia la dorsal

facts.statement: It possessed two sacral vertebrae and 45 caudal vertebrae of decreasing size.
facts.quote: Poseía dos vértebras sacras y 45 vértebras caudales de tamaño decreciente

facts.statement: It had a marked reduction in forelimbs that were 40% shorter than the hindlimbs.
facts.quote: Gracilisuchus poseía una marcada reducción de los miembros anteriores que eran un 40% menores que los miembros posteriores

facts.statement: It was protected by a double row of bony plates running from its spine to the tail tip.
facts.quote: protegido por una fila doble de las placas óseas que recorrían su espina dorsal hasta la extremidad de la cola

facts.statement: It was a small predator whose diet consisted mainly of insects and small vertebrates.
facts.quote: Se trató de un pequeño depredador cuyo principal alimento estaría constituido principalmente de insectos y vertebrados pequeños

facts.statement: Researchers believe it could run upright on its hind legs.
facts.quote: por lo que se piensa que podía correr erguido en sus patas traseras

facts.statement: It was described by A. S. Romer in 1972.
facts.quote: Fue descrito por A. S. Romer en 1972

facts.statement: Its remains were found in the Los Chañares Formation in the Cuyo region of La Rioja Province, Argentina.
facts.quote: Sus restos se encontraron en la Formación Los Chañares de la Provincia de La Rioja, en la región cuyana de la Argentina

facts.statement: It lived in the middle Triassic, during the Anisian and Ladinian stages, approximately 240 to 235 million years ago.
facts.quote: vivió a mediados del período Triásico, en el Anisiense y Ladiniense hace aproximadamente entre 240 y 235 millones de años

facts.statement: Its time range is estimated from 241.464 to 237 million years ago during the Ladinian.
facts.quote: Time range: Ladinian to Ladinian (241.464 to 237 million years ago)

facts.statement: It is now considered a sister taxon to the Crocodylomorpha.
facts.quote: ahora se le considera un taxón hermano de los Crocodylomorpha

facts.statement: Romer initially reconstructed Gracilisuchus as a facultative biped, though this interpretation was based on material later reassigned.
facts.quote: Romer reconstructed Gracilisuchus as a facultative biped in his initial description

facts.statement: Remains of Gracilisuchus and other tetrapods were found within carbonate concretions in the rock.
facts.quote: It is in these concretions that the remains of Gracilisuchus and other tetrapods have been found

facts.statement: Uranium-lead dating of Chañares deposits in 2016 indicated an early Carnian age of 236 to 234 million years.
facts.quote: uranium-lead dating of Chañares deposits in 2016, indicating an early Carnian age of 236 to 234 million years

facts.statement: For a time, it was considered a dinosaur.
facts.quote: por un tiempo fue considerado un dinosaurio
